jd:
AI Product Manager — Youth AI Learning Experience

A fictional education company is building an AI learning companion for teenagers and families. The product helps students explore difficult topics, draft study plans, and ask follow-up questions while giving adults understandable controls. The product manager will interview students, caregivers, and educators, then decide which learning and safety problems deserve the next release. They will define age-appropriate interaction rules, consent and escalation paths, and a clear way for users to report troubling answers. They will work with design, policy, trust, and engineering partners to decide where a human response is necessary.

The role calls for a roadmap that improves useful learning without encouraging over-reliance or exposing private information. Success measures include meaningful learning sessions, repeat use, complaints, safety escalations, and user comprehension of controls. A strong candidate can translate conflicting user needs into explicit tradeoffs, test a feature with a small cohort, explain its limitations, and use qualitative feedback alongside numbers. Prior product ownership in consumer or education experiences would be relevant. This is an original fictional evaluation card inspired by a public PM role, not that employer's job description.
profile:
Candidate RL-P11 | Advertising Product Associate

Experience: At a commerce advertising platform, I support the team that helps small sellers understand campaign performance. Interviews with sellers showed that the dashboard used agency terminology they did not recognise. I rewrote the reporting labels, drafted examples for common decisions, and worked with an analyst to define consistent attribution windows. The new report was used more often in the pilot group, but I cannot claim it improved return on ad spend; budgets shifted during the test.

I coordinated an experiment on suggested campaign descriptions. The creative team wrote the review criteria, and I collected cases in which the generated copy implied discounts that did not exist. We kept the feature in an opt-in internal tool while the review process matured. I did not build the model, and I would not describe that trial as an autonomous campaign optimiser. My day-to-day work includes backlog refinement, stakeholder updates, customer calls, and checking data definitions before release.

Education and tools: Marketing and statistics degree. I use SQL, spreadsheets, Figma, campaign reporting tools, and simple Python for CSV quality checks. I care about separating attractive dashboards from decisions sellers can actually make.

jd:
AI Product Manager — Shared Workplace Assistant

A fictional workplace software company wants its assistant to help teams coordinate inside chat and document tools. Unlike a private chatbot, this assistant can be mentioned by several colleagues, summarize a shared thread, and suggest next actions that everyone can inspect. The product manager will study how teams hand off work, identify moments where an agent genuinely saves time, and define interaction rules for asking permission before consequential actions. They will shape onboarding for early customers and work with partner platforms on integration requirements and launch plans.

The PM will choose which surfaces to support first, how to show uncertainty and source context, and how permissions should limit what the assistant can read or share. Product measures could include activated teams, completed collaborative tasks, repeated use, correction rates, and support incidents. The candidate should be able to run customer discovery, prioritize a roadmap across different team sizes, and coordinate design, security, engineering, and partner teams. They should make adoption decisions using both user interviews and measured behavior. This role card is fictional and originally worded; the linked public posting supplies only the role-family context.
profile:
Candidate RL-P12 | Connected Device Product Manager

Experience: I have managed software features for a home-energy monitor for three years. Customers complained that alerts arrived after they had already changed appliance use. I visited installation partners, analysed event timestamps, and proposed a shorter alert path plus clearer explanations of uncertainty. Engineers improved device buffering while I changed notification rules. Alerts arrived sooner in lab and field checks, although we do not yet know whether households saved more energy.

Before product management I was a test engineer and wrote scripts to replay device messages. That background helps me discuss sensor failures, battery constraints, and release rollback plans. I took part in a forecast feature review, comparing model outputs with actual meter readings for different home types. A specialist team trained the forecast model; I defined the customer-facing interval and made sure the interface did not display a false precision. I have not worked with language-model retrieval.

Education and tools: Electrical engineering degree, six years in hardware and software teams. I use Python, SQL, prototype dashboards, field notes, and structured release checklists. I often choose reliability fixes ahead of a new feature when home conditions vary from a demo.

jd_source_title: Lead Product Manager - AI Agents & Emerging Products
jd:
AI Product Manager — Consumer Agent Subscription

A fictional consumer app offers an AI agent that helps people organize personal projects and follow through on small tasks. The company is considering a paid plan, but users currently try the agent once and rarely return. The product manager will investigate whether the problem is weak task value, confusing setup, poor reliability, or unclear pricing. They will speak with new and retained users, map the activation journey, and propose a focused experiment rather than adding a long list of features.

The PM owns the product direction from early validation through launch. They will decide which agent actions need user approval, how to communicate failures, which benefits belong in a free or paid tier, and how to compare acquisition cost with recurring value. They will partner with design, marketing, finance, analytics, and engineering to test onboarding and subscription changes. Success measures include task completion, week-four retention, conversion, cancellation reasons, refunds, and customer support load. The candidate needs evidence-led prioritization, sound consumer product judgment, and the ability to explain tradeoffs between growth, user trust, and AI operating cost. This synthetic role is not an employer vacancy.
profile:
Candidate RL-P13 | Marketplace Product Manager

Experience: At a travel booking marketplace, I look after the post-booking experience for guests and hosts. I reviewed support conversations to understand why check-in instructions failed and spoke with hosts in three regions. The team redesigned where access details appear and added a reminder for hosts to verify them. Contact volume per booking declined in the trial, but travel mix changed between the comparison periods. I recorded that caveat in the launch note.

I evaluated a vendor translation feature for host messages. Native-language reviewers found polite but incorrect references to local transport and access codes. I prioritised a human correction path and blocked automatic sending for time-critical instructions. The implementation team owned the model integration. My contribution was deciding which communications were safe to automate and which needed confirmation. I have also written marketplace rules for dispute escalation and worked with trust staff when a simple conversion target conflicted with guest safety.

Education and tools: BA in international business; four years in product roles. I use SQL, product analytics, interview guides, Figma, and multilingual content review. I would like to build stronger technical depth in AI evaluation and retrieval.

jd:
AI Product Manager — Conversational Service Assurance

A fictional B2B company helps contact centers check whether their AI voice and chat assistants handle customer requests reliably. Buyers complain that simple demos look good while real multi-turn conversations fail silently. The product manager will interview operations leaders and frontline agents, define the highest-cost failure types, and prioritize a product that lets customers create realistic test scenarios, review evidence, and decide when a release is safe enough to deploy. They will distinguish automated test signals from cases that still need a human reviewer.

The PM will own a roadmap covering setup, test coverage, issue triage, and reporting. They will decide how to communicate uncertainty when a test misses a rare but serious problem. They will coordinate with sales, customer success, design, engineering, and legal so the product fits real approval workflows. Measures include defect discovery before launch, false alarms, time to resolve, customer adoption, renewal, and evaluator agreement on sampled cases. A strong candidate can turn ambiguous customer complaints into clear requirements, run structured pilots, and give commercial teams an honest product narrative. This is an original synthetic PM card based on a public role family.
profile:
Candidate RL-P14 | People Systems Product Specialist

Experience: I work on internal mobility tools at an enterprise software firm. Employees previously had to search several pages to find eligibility rules for open roles. I mapped the content with human-resources partners, redesigned filters, and ran task-based usability sessions. People found policy information faster in the sessions; I have no evidence yet that internal hiring improved. I maintained the rule owner and review date for each page to prevent stale guidance.

The team investigated whether skill suggestions could help employees explore roles. I set up a workshop with employees from non-traditional career paths and found that job titles were a poor proxy for experience. I wrote requirements for editable skill evidence and a way to challenge suggestions. A data-science team built a prototype; I reviewed examples of false positives and missing experience. It has not been used for hiring decisions. I understand the fairness concerns from this work but have not run a formal bias audit.

Education and tools: Psychology degree and five years in HR operations and product. I use interviews, SQL extracts, survey analysis, and prototyping tools. I prefer employee-controlled recommendations over opaque scoring.

jd:
AI Product Manager — Team Knowledge Workspace

A fictional company is replacing scattered internal documents and chat searches with one workplace where people and AI assistants plan projects together. The product manager will observe how employees locate decisions, request access, and pass work between teams. They will choose an initial workflow where an assistant can summarize context and propose actions without crossing document permissions or obscuring who made a decision. Research with different departments should reveal what can be shared, what must stay restricted, and where the current workflow breaks down.

The PM owns the product vision, a short roadmap, and measurable outcomes. They will partner with security, operations, design, and engineering to define consent, audit, and escalation behavior. They will test adoption in a small group before wider rollout and compare actual task success with satisfaction surveys and support tickets. Measures could include weekly active teams, successful handoffs, time to find a decision, incorrect access attempts, and trust-related complaints. The candidate should show strong user discovery, prioritization under limited capacity, and judgment about AI behavior in sensitive team workflows. This is an invented PM role card informed by a public posting, not copied from it.
profile:
Candidate RL-P15 | Community Product Manager

Experience: At a multiplayer game studio, I own parts of the player-reporting flow and moderator console. I observed moderators working through busy weekend queues and redesigned the evidence summary so they could see context before acting. In a six-week pilot, median review time fell, while overturn rates remained similar. I checked a sample of decisions because speed alone would have been a poor measure of success.

I partnered with a safety engineer on a classifier that routed obvious spam reports to a separate queue. My role was defining routing thresholds, escalation rules, and feedback from moderators. I did not train the classifier. The team left harassment complaints under human review, particularly when slang or friendship groups changed the meaning of a message. I have written policy-facing explanations for players and coordinated with localisation specialists across regions. An early generative reply draft was withdrawn after it suggested actions moderators were not authorised to take.

Education and tools: Sociology degree, community operations background, four years in product. I use event analytics, SQL, user interviews, Figma, and incident reviews. I am comfortable defending a slower workflow when it protects appeal rights.

jd_source_title: Principal, Product Manager-Tech, eShop Premium Ads CX
jd:
Commercial Product Manager — Sponsored Retail Discovery

A fictional shopping marketplace sells sponsored placements on product pages and in category feeds. Advertisers want more measurable sales, while shoppers complain that some sponsored items interrupt discovery. The product manager will research both sides of the marketplace and decide where ads can create useful discovery without overwhelming organic results. They will define the product requirements for new placements, advertiser controls, and reporting, then coordinate experiments with design, sales, analytics, and engineering.

The PM must choose guardrails before launch: relevance thresholds, disclosure, frequency limits, and ways to investigate complaints. They will compare revenue and advertiser return with shopper engagement and long-term trust. Success measures could include incremental advertiser sales, repeat campaign purchase, shopper conversion, session abandonment, ad-related complaints, and placement fill. A strong candidate can write a concise business case, make tradeoffs among stakeholders, and interpret A/B results without claiming that every revenue increase is beneficial. Familiarity with ads products and customer research matters more than writing the ranking algorithm. This is an originally written fictional card inspired by an official product-management posting.
profile:
Candidate RL-P21 | Service Improvement Lead

Recent work: I look after the questions people ask while setting up accounts at a business-software cooperative. The old help journey sent the same question to three different teams. I listened to call recordings, collected examples where written guidance disagreed with the product, and made a single review queue with named owners. The team now resolves a greater share of routine questions in one contact, according to weekly service reports.

We also tried a writing assistant that assembled draft answers from reviewed help pages. I drew up 65 examples of the awkward questions, marked which ones required a person to decide, and compared drafts with the exact policy page available at the time. When the tool combined two policies, I asked engineers to show the passage it used and to pause instead of guessing. I did not choose the underlying provider. My role was deciding what the service should say and proving when it should stay silent.

Before this I coordinated accessibility fixes for an online learning service. I have a humanities degree, some spreadsheet and database-query experience, and no formal product-manager title. Colleagues describe me as patient in workshops and strict about the wording that reaches customers.

jd_source_title: Sr. Product Manager - Tech, India Ads
jd:
Commercial Product Manager — Regional Advertiser Growth

A fictional commerce platform is expanding self-service advertising to smaller merchants across several regional markets. Many merchants create an account but never launch a campaign, and some who do spend once without returning. The product manager will interview advertisers and account teams to learn whether budget risk, setup effort, weak measurement, or unclear value causes these drop-offs. They will segment merchants by maturity and choose an initial product change that can be tested in one market before rollout.

The PM owns advertiser onboarding, budget guidance, campaign feedback, and launch coordination with sales and marketing. They will work with analytics and engineering on product requirements but are accountable for customer outcomes and tradeoffs, not model training or coding. Success measures include activation, retained advertisers, meaningful spend, advertiser return, merchant support contacts, and shopper relevance. The role requires the ability to combine funnel data with interviews, define experiments, and adapt a global ads product to local merchant needs without fragmenting the experience. The fictional employer and wording are original; the source link establishes only a real PM job family.
profile:
Candidate RL-P22 | Business Development Coordinator

Summary: Interested in AI product management, generative AI, agents, RAG, prompt engineering, responsible AI, machine learning, A/B testing, SQL, Python, strategy, roadmaps, OKRs, and stakeholder management. These topics are listed in the online courses I have watched and in the role descriptions I am using to plan my next move. I want to be transparent that the list is an interest inventory, not a list of delivered projects.

Work history: For two years I have booked demonstrations for a office-software reseller. I maintain contact records, prepare slides for account executives, and collect customer questions after sales calls. Last year I suggested a new demo order based on common objections; the sales manager approved it, but I did not measure a before-and-after outcome. I do not own a software backlog or meet with engineers. An AI sales-assistant vendor showed us a prototype. I attended the session but did not evaluate the model.

Education: Business diploma and several short online AI courses with quizzes. I can use spreadsheets and presentation software. I have not yet written SQL or Python outside guided lessons and would need support to run an experiment or design a product requirement.

jd:
Commercial Product Manager — Subscription Value and Conversion

A fictional media service offers a free tier and a paid membership with additional listening benefits. Research suggests users know that Premium exists but cannot explain why the price is worthwhile. The product manager will examine the journey from first use to consideration, interview free users who did and did not subscribe, and decide how to make the paid value clear at relevant moments. The PM will work with design, marketing, research, finance, and regional teams on a small set of experience and messaging experiments.

The role covers the value proposition, upgrade entry points, and local-market adaptation. The PM should avoid manipulative prompts that temporarily raise conversions while increasing cancellations or support complaints. They will set a baseline, design A/B tests, and monitor conversion, retained subscribers, lifetime value, cancellation reasons, and satisfaction by cohort. A strong candidate can reason about willingness to pay, prioritize across markets, and explain how product changes differ from marketing claims. They should use both quantitative funnel evidence and direct user feedback to decide what to launch. This is a fictional, originally worded product role card informed by a public subscriptions PM posting.
profile:
Candidate RL-P26 | Junior Product Coordinator

Experience: At an accounting software provider I coordinate release notes, collect support tickets, and arrange user interviews for the product manager. I have written acceptance criteria for two small settings changes after watching the PM do earlier examples. I did not set priorities for the wider roadmap. A cross-team project reduced the number of billing questions, but my work was limited to updating help copy and checking that links worked; I do not claim ownership of the outcome.

My university project proposed a retrieval-based assistant for invoice terminology. I assembled a small set of public definitions and manually compared 20 generated answers to the source text. It was a classroom prototype. It was never used by customers, had no privacy review, and was not monitored after the demo. I have not built an agent, trained a model, or managed a live AI release. I have watched tutorials on these topics and want to learn them properly.

Education and tools: Business information systems degree. I am comfortable in Figma and spreadsheets. I can read a basic SQL query but have not written one for production analysis. I value clear task notes and asking for review when a claim exceeds my evidence.

jd:
Commercial Product Manager — Creator Memberships

A fictional creator platform is considering a membership tier that offers fans extra experiences and gives creators a more predictable income stream. The product manager will research what fans value, what creators can consistently deliver, and whether a single plan or flexible tiers fit different communities. They will define the first release, including discovery, benefits, pricing presentation, and cancellation. They will coordinate with creator relations, payments, design, data, and engineering while keeping the experience understandable on both sides of the marketplace.

The PM will judge success through subscriber conversion, retained members, creator participation, average revenue, benefit use, complaints, and refund rates. They will test whether early growth comes from genuine value or short-lived promotion and adjust the roadmap accordingly. Decisions should consider younger users, regional payment expectations, creator workload, and the effect of membership features on free community participation. The candidate needs product discovery, pricing judgment, experiment design, and cross-functional communication; engineering implementation remains with the engineering team. This is an original synthetic PM scenario informed by an official subscriptions role, not a copied job advertisement.
profile:
Candidate RL-P24 | Education Researcher seeking Product Role

Research history: I spent six years studying how adults learn technical skills at a research institute. I designed interview protocols, recruited participants, analysed transcripts, and published reports for programme managers. In one study I combined surveys with course-completion records and found that shorter practice sessions correlated with higher completion. We did not randomise assignment, so I cautioned against claiming the shorter sessions caused the result.

Practical projects: I volunteered with a small nonprofit to redesign an application form for learners. I observed five users, sketched alternatives, and tested the revised wording. The nonprofit adopted part of the proposal, but I was not involved in its software implementation or later metrics. I also took a semester course on language models and built a local notebook that compared answers to a handful of education-policy questions. It was a class exercise, not a deployed service.

I want to move into AI product work because I enjoy translating research into decisions. I can bring careful evidence gathering and communication, but I have not managed engineers, a product budget, or a live feature. Tools include qualitative coding software, R, spreadsheets, and basic Python.

jd_source_title: Product Manager, New Markets and Monetization
jd:
Commercial Product Manager — AI Service Monetization

A fictional AI service sells usage-based access to organizations through direct accounts and partner channels. Customers say it is hard to predict spending, while partners struggle to reconcile usage with invoices. The product manager will study buyers, finance teams, and resellers to find the most costly sources of confusion. They will define a roadmap for spend visibility, understandable limits, partner attribution, and pricing packages that support new industries without creating hidden costs or billing disputes.

The PM will write commercial product requirements and work with finance, legal, sales, design, analytics, and engineering on release decisions. They should distinguish a pricing policy change from a product feature and explain the consequences of both. Success measures include billing disputes, time to first paid use, partner activation, revenue retention, customer support effort, and forecast error. The candidate should be able to map the customer journey, test packaging with buyers, and make clear choices when growth opportunities conflict with trust or implementation cost. Technical fluency helps in discussing usage data, but this is a product ownership role rather than an engineering or algorithm position. This fictional card is independently written from a public PM role theme.
profile:
Candidate RL-P25 | Growth Project Lead

Profile: I have supported launches for a consumer finance app and often present myself as a product-minded growth lead. During a referral campaign, sign-ups increased by 32 percent. I built the weekly report and suggested one change to the invitation copy; several teams also altered incentives, paid-media spend, and landing pages. I do not have an estimate of what my copy change contributed. I was not responsible for the product backlog, although I attended some planning meetings.

My strongest work is interviewing prospective customers about why they hesitate to finish registration. I coded 25 interviews and shared three themes with designers, who changed a disclosure screen. I did not observe the later user test. I have used a text generator to prepare first drafts of survey questions, which a researcher reviewed. I have not built or evaluated an AI feature for customers. My slides mention conversion optimisation, segmentation, personalisation, and experimentation, but those terms refer to campaign operations rather than controlled product tests.

Education and tools: Communications degree, four years in growth roles, spreadsheet reporting, CRM systems, and dashboard reading. I can write clearly and work across teams; I would need coaching to own technical delivery and rigorous causal measurement.
